identification.summary: Hellsing is a small cyberespionage group named by Kaspersky in April 2015 that targeted mostly government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S1][S2]. Kaspersky found it while tracing Naikon, after a Naikon spear-phishing target questioned the email, declined to open the attachment, and sent a malicious email back to the sender [S2][S3]. Kaspersky estimated that close to 20 organizations were targeted [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Active since at least 2012 [S3]. Publicly disclosed by Kaspersky in April 2015 [S2].
identification.notes: Malpedia (via the imported MISP Galaxy text) says the actor seems to have targeted APT30 and possibly uses the same infrastructure as Mirage [S6]. Press reporting of Kaspersky's analysis says Kaspersky saw infrastructure overlap with PlayfullDragon (GREF) and Mirage (Vixen Panda) and treated Hellsing as a stand-alone operation [S7]. These are vendor-cluster overlaps, not mergers. No Microsoft Threat Intelligence name or MITRE ATT&CK group was found for Hellsing in the searches run.

attribution.sponsor: China (suspected). The Council on Foreign Relations Cyber Operations Tracker lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S5].
attribution.confidence: Low-to-moderate, and not stated in numeric form by any source seen. The CFR tracker lists the sponsor as suspected [S5]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: CFR's tracker classifies the activity as espionage and names China as suspected sponsor [S5]. Kaspersky's public reporting describes the victimology as government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S2]. Infrastructure overlap with other China-linked clusters (Mirage) is reported by Malpedia and press coverage [S6][S7]. The specific technical evidence behind the China attribution is in the Securelist report, which could not be opened.

objectives: Cyberespionage against government and diplomatic organizations in Asia [S1][S2]. The counter-attack on Naikon suggests an additional goal of identifying that group and gathering intelligence on it, in Kaspersky's assessment [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Kaspersky detected malware mainly in Malaysia and the Philippines, with detections also in India, Indonesia and the US; the US detections were tied to diplomatic agencies and India to older malware versions [S1]. CFR lists suspected victims in Malaysia, the Philippines, India, Indonesia and the US [S5]. Malpedia describes spear-phishing against diplomatic targets in Southeast Asia, India and the US [S6].

capabilities.summary: Spear-phishing emails carrying archives with malware, similar to the approach used against Naikon [S1]. Lures included password-protected RAR archives, which help bypass malware scanners, with SCR or other executables inside [S1]. The custom backdoor can download and upload files, update itself and uninstall itself [S2][S3]. Malpedia lists PlugX among associated malware families [S6]. Kaspersky described the group as small and technically unremarkable [S2].

campaigns.name: Earliest known activity
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky and press coverage state that Hellsing has been active since at least 2012, mainly against government organizations in Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines.

campaigns.name: Counter-attack on Naikon and public disclosure
campaigns.summary: A Naikon spear-phishing target questioned the sender and returned a malicious email. This led Kaspersky to discover Hellsing, which it described as an APT-on-APT incident and the start of 'APT wars'. Kaspersky judged the reply aimed to identify Naikon and gather intelligence on it.

campaigns.name: Spear-phishing against Asian government and diplomatic targets
campaigns.summary: Close to 20 organizations were estimated targeted, mostly in Malaysia and the Philippines, with some in India, Indonesia and the US.

diamond.adversary: Small, suspected China-based espionage group; no individuals or organizations named in the sources seen [S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with password-protected RAR archives containing executables; custom backdoor with file transfer and self-update/uninstall functions [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Possible shared infrastructure with Mirage, and reported overlap with PlayfullDragon [S6][S7]. Indicators are published in the Securelist report, which could not be opened [S1].
diamond.victim: Government and diplomatic organizations, mainly in Malaysia and the Philippines, plus the Naikon group [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Regional diplomatic and government intelligence collection in Southeast Asia, India and the US, with a rivalry element against Naikon [S2][S5].
diamond.technology: Email and attachment handling; password-protected archives that evade scanners [S1].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach securelist.com, kaspersky.com, cfr.org or theregister.com (DNS failure), so the primary Securelist report was read only through search-result summaries. Technical detail (malware family names, C2 infrastructure, IOCs, timeline) is therefore not captured.
No Microsoft name, MITRE ATT&CK group ID or government attribution was found for Hellsing.
Evidence basis for the suspected China sponsorship is not visible in the sources gathered.

Cluster boundaries are unresolved: reported overlaps with Mirage, APT30, PlayfullDragon and Naikon were seen only through secondary summaries. One search summary also said Kaspersky reported the Hellsing developer started from Cycldek sources; this was not verified against the report text.
Activity after 2015 is not documented in the sources gathered. Malpedia's reference list was not fully visible.
Malpedia page date is not shown; its source entry uses the retrieval date.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Government and diplomatic email systems in the Indo-Pacific, and partner-nation diplomatic staff, are key terrain [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor is small and technically unremarkable, so it relies on social engineering rather than novel exploits [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phish with a password-protected archive, then a custom backdoor that uploads files [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued diplomatic and government collection in Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia and India, with opportunistic US diplomatic targeting. MDCOA is use of the same lure style against US or partner defense staff during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: password-protected RAR emails containing SCR files, and backdoor beaconing from government workstations [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track phishing against partner diplomatic and government networks; Kaspersky's IOCs are on Securelist and should be pulled and validated [S1]. (2) Authorities: monitoring of partner-nation networks depends on partner agreements; no US authority is implied by the sources. (3) Mission assurance: block or sandbox password-protected archives and SCR attachments on mission networks [S1]. (4) Coordination: overlap with other China-linked clusters means shared reporting with partners and vendors is needed before any attribution is used [S6][S7].
